content: The health effects of tobacco smoking are profound and multifaceted, impacting both direct smokers and those exposed to secondhand smoke. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated in 2002 that smoking was responsible for 26% of male deaths and 9% of female deaths in developed countries. Similarly, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has described tobacco use as the leading preventable risk to human health in developed nations and a major cause of premature death worldwide. Smokers, on average, live 5 to 10 years less than non-smokers. Approximately half of male smokers will die from smoking-related illnesses. WHO has projected that tobacco could kill one billion people this century. The primary health risks associated with tobacco smoking include cardiovascular diseases, such as myocardial infarction (heart attack), respiratory diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and emphysema, and various cancers, particularly lung cancer, as well as cancers of the larynx and mouth. Before World War I, lung cancer was considered rare, but the post-war rise in cigarette smoking led to an epidemic of lung cancer. Among individuals who have ever smoked, nearly one in ten will develop lung cancer, and one in six men who continue smoking will develop the disease. In contrast, only one in seventy-five lifelong non-smokers will develop lung cancer. Male smokers are also 85% more likely to experience impotence compared to non-smokers, with smoking being a significant cause of erectile dysfunction due to arterial narrowing. The risk of developing smoking-related diseases is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of smoking. However, cessation of smoking leads to a gradual decrease in these risks as the body begins to repair itself. Smoking-related diseases include various cancers (lung, kidney, larynx, head and neck, breast, bladder, esophagus, pancreas, stomach, and others), cardiovascular diseases (stroke, peripheral vascular disease), respiratory ailments (chronic bronchitis, emphysema), birth defects in offspring of pregnant smokers, Buerger's disease, cataracts, cognitive dysfunction, and increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Smoking also reduces memory and cognitive abilities, particularly in adolescents. Cigar and pipe smokers, while inhaling less smoke than cigarette smokers, still face significantly higher risks of lung cancer compared to non-smokers. They are also at risk for cancers of the oral cavity, larynx, and esophagus. Chewing tobacco is similarly carcinogenic, with risks for cancers of the mouth and jaw. The benefits of smoking cessation are immediate, including normalization of blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature, improved circulation, and enhanced senses of smell and taste. Tobacco smoke contains approximately 3,000 chemicals, many of which are biologically active and harmful. Long-term exposure to compounds like carbon monoxide and cyanide damages lung and arterial tissues, contributing to cardiovascular diseases and loss of elasticity in the alveoli, leading to emphysema and COPD. Additionally, tobacco contains radioactive carcinogens such as lead-210 and polonium-210, which accumulate in the lungs and other tissues, causing significant radiation exposure and increasing the risk of lung cancer. These radioactive elements are absorbed from the soil and fertilizers used in tobacco cultivation. Nicotine, a potent stimulant, is the primary addictive component of tobacco. Despite being present in small amounts in inhaled smoke, it is sufficient to cause physical and psychological dependence. Nicotine is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, reaching the brain within 10 seconds of inhalation, which reinforces the addictive behavior. Withdrawal symptoms include irritability, jitteriness, dry mouth, rapid heartbeat, insomnia, and mild depression. While physical dependence on nicotine subsides within 10 to 20 days of cessation, psychological dependence can persist for months or years. Smoking also significantly increases the risk of heart disease by narrowing blood vessels and promoting blockages, which can lead to heart attacks or strokes. Chemicals in tobacco smoke can damage arterial walls, facilitating cholesterol buildup and further increasing cardiovascular risks. Smoking during pregnancy is associated with spontaneous abortion, fetal health risks, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). Secondhand smoke exposure also poses significant risks to fetuses and infants. Epidemiological studies, such as the British Doctors Study, have demonstrated that smoking reduces life expectancy by 10 years and that nearly half of smokers die from smoking-related diseases. Smoking prevalence is higher among lower socioeconomic groups, contributing to disparities in life expectancy. There is no credible evidence that low tar or light cigarettes are safer than regular cigarettes. Cigar smoking, even without inhalation, carries significant health risks, including cancers of the oral cavity, esophagus, and lungs. Pipe smoking also poses risks, particularly for oral cancer. While some studies have suggested potential protective effects of smoking against certain conditions like Parkinson's disease or ulcerative colitis, these findings are often confounded by other factors, such as differential mortality rates. Smoking remains the leading preventable cause of illness and death worldwide, with devastating effects on both individual and public health.
